title: Genuine Encouragement
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. argues that the way out of a teacher's seasonal discouragement is often to encourage someone else rather than to try to lift oneself. He supports this with four specific moments from a single week, involving students and a student's father, in which he named something true and admirable about a person. He admits he often fumbles the words, but holds that the cost is minimal and the upside large. The essay presents encouragement as a daily action available regardless of school setting or policy. It closes by linking encouragement to students' sense of belonging in class, which he calls an important noncognitive factor.
points: When morale sags, the essay's counterintuitive advice is that the way up is down: encourage others instead of trying to pep-talk yourself.
The encouragement has to be genuine and specific, as in telling a student what he admires about their character or telling a parent what his parenting has produced.
Stuart models the practice with four concrete examples from one week, showing it takes minutes and no special setting.
He ties encouragement to belonging, treating it as a lever on a noncognitive factor in student success and not just a mood boost.
quotes: What I mean is that rather than trying to encourage myself up and out of a slump like this, it often helps me most to encourage others. The key, of course, is for the encouragement to be genuine.

If you're like me, seasons of discouragement come along at some point in a school year. We get tired, we get behind, we get frustrated, we experience setbacks. These things accrue, and it becomes easier and easier to hit the snooze button.

As I was doing it, I told her that she was the kind of young lady I pray my daughters will be one day: pleasant, hard-working, earnest about school, drama-free. She said it was the best compliment she'd ever received — which just shows you how pleasant and kind she is.

Seeing him so excited and focused and practical was exciting for me and something I had been hoping and praying for for him since he was a ninth grader. I told him as much, and told him to keep up the good work. I could tell that the words meant something to him as they had to me.
There isn't anything stupendous or Hollywood-esque in these moments of genuine encouragement. I almost always feel like I am tripping over my words and poorly communicating what I intend.

The time cost is minimal, and the upside is huge — because who knows what that shot in the arm will lead the person we're encouraging to go and do. These are the kinds of daily actions we all have available to us, regardless of the teaching situation, the school setting, or the prevailing policies.
Encouragement is always an option. It is likely, too, to increase our students' sense that they belong in our classes — an important noncognitive factor.
